note: Bibliographic register. Every entry used to support a factual statement in the atlas. Entries marked kind=press or kind=museum are used for specific documented details and are identified as such where they appear. Page references are given only where the page was actually consulted.

entries.author: Merridale, Catherine
entries.title: Night of Stone: Death and Memory in Russia
entries.supports: Twentieth-century death, mourning and memory in Russia; the argument that public and private mourning diverged. Used for interpretation, not as a source of statistics.
entries.limitation: A work of synthesis and interviews; figures given in it should be checked against the specialist literature.

entries.author: Zelenin, Dmitry K.
entries.title: Очерки русской мифологии. Вып. 1: Умершие неестественною смертью и русалки
entries.title_en: Essays in Russian Mythology, part 1: Those Who Died an Unnatural Death, and Rusalki
entries.edition_used: Reprint: Izbrannye trudy / Ocherki russkoi mifologii, Moscow: Indrik, 1995 (ed. E. E. Levkievskaia, intro. N. I. Tolstoi); chapter 4 (Semik), about pp. 129–138, read in an unofficial online copy
entries.supports: Zelenin’s compilation of reports that people who died an ‘unnatural’ death were buried away from the churchyard, including the two local cases used on plate N: a forest ravine near Orkino (Saratov uezd) and a ‘deaf forest ravine’ in Silinskaya volost (Simbirsk guberniya); his term ‘zalozhnye’ for the ‘unclean’ dead and his reading of them as rusalki, as the later studies read for this atlas report them. On plate O: what he reports for Semik in Smolensk province and for the poor-house burial sites of Vyatka (Khlynov, Kotelnich, Ledovo).
entries.limitation: Only part of the book was read: chapter 4, ‘Commemoration of the zalozhnye at Semik’ (sections 34–36), through a summary of an online copy of the 1995 reprint, not line by line. Page numbers for the authorities he cites (Dobrovolsky 1908, Georgievsky 1894, Veshchomov, Glushkov, Zelenin 1904) are as that reading gave them and are second-hand: the originals were not seen. Elsewhere the term, the category and the rusalka reading are taken from later authors who cite him, and the two local cases on plate N were read as excerpts. The Orkino report concerns half-Russified Mordvins, not Russians. The compilation is over a century old; the category is Zelenin’s construction, and later scholarship disputes its coherence and the rusalka derivation.

entries.author: Ivanits, Linda J.
entries.title: Russian Folk Belief
entries.supports: Folk beliefs about the soul, the dead, household spirits and the unclean dead; the general account of funeral and memorial custom used in plates A–D.
entries.limitation: A survey of the published ethnographic literature, not a regional field study.

entries.author: Barsov, Elpidifor Vasil’evich
entries.title: Prichitaniia Severnogo kraia
entries.title_en: Laments of the Northern Land
entries.supports: The foundational collection of Russian funeral laments, recorded in the Olonets region: the arrangement of laments by kinship of the dead, the role of the professional lamenter (voplenitsa), the performance occasions.
entries.limitation: Volume 1 (1872): contents page and introduction pp. I–III read through the Internet Archive OCR text; the funeral-customs passages pp. 303–313, the introduction pp. VIII–IX and the performer register pp. 313–327 checked against page images (the images come from the owner’s archive, not fetched here). The heading of the performer on p. 326 is blurred in the scan; the surname is read as Momokova from the OCR layer, and the spelling Momonova is not excluded. Reading status: RELEVANT EXTRACT READ; volumes 2–3 and the lament texts themselves not read. OCR is uncollated; page numbers for the contents come from the OCR and may be off. No lament verse is printed in the atlas.

entries.author: Baiburin, Albert Kashfullovich
entries.title: Ritual v traditsionnoi kul’ture
entries.title_en: Ritual in Traditional Culture
entries.supports: Ritual as a sign system; the critique of reading rites as survivals of earlier religion.
entries.limitation: Theoretical; used here for the critique, not for regional description.

entries.author: Tolstoy, Nikita I. (ed.); Tolstaia, Svetlana M. (ed., vol. 5)
entries.title: Slavianskie drevnosti: Etnolingvisticheskii slovar’
entries.title_en: Slavic Antiquities: An Ethnolinguistic Dictionary
entries.supports: Terminology and comparative context for Slavic funerary customs; used for definitions, not for page-specific claims.
entries.limitation: Covers all Slavic traditions. Any statement taken from it must be checked against its local attribution; the atlas uses it only for general definitions.

entries.author: Veniamin (Krasnopevkov-Rumovskii), Archbishop
entries.title: Novaia Skrizhal’
entries.title_en: The New Tablet
entries.supports: Ch. XXIII § 2: the reasons for commemoration on the third, ninth and fortieth days (Neophyte of Rhodes, Simeon of Thessalonica, the handbook’s own); the body-decay explanation it sets aside; § 3 on kutia; ch. XX § 15 on wailing at funerals.
entries.limitation: Read in the azbyka.ru online edition: ch. XXIII §§ 2–3 (§ 3 to its first lines) and ch. XX § 15; the rest of the book not read. An early nineteenth-century handbook for clergy and laity: it describes the normative rite and quotes earlier authorities, not household practice. The first publication year is as given in the earlier register.

entries.author: Shevzov, Vera
entries.title: Russian Orthodoxy on the Eve of Revolution
entries.supports: Parish life and lay religious practice in late imperial Russia, including the social organisation of commemoration.
entries.limitation: Focused on the late imperial period; not a source for Soviet or post-Soviet practice.

entries.author: Pravoslavnaia entsiklopediia (Orthodox Encyclopedia)
entries.title: Nadgrobie
entries.title_en: Grave monument
entries.supports: Peter I’s decree of 10 October 1723 on burial inside towns; the history of the grave monument.
entries.limitation: An encyclopedia entry; used for the decree and its date, not for the wider interpretation.

entries.author: Mos.ru (official portal of the city of Moscow)
entries.title: Material on the history of Vagankovo Cemetery
entries.supports: The founding of Vagankovo in 1771 for victims of plague; the role of Grigorii Orlov’s commission; the burial of unnamed Muscovites.
entries.limitation: A municipal historical note, not a peer-reviewed study. Figures are not given beyond ‘thousands’. The PDF could not be re-fetched on 2026-11-16 (not on the session allowlist); the support line is from the earlier reading.

entries.author: Mos.ru / Glavnoe arkhivnoe upravlenie goroda Moskvy
entries.title: Material on the history of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
entries.supports: Architects (Burdin, Klimov, Rabaev), sculptor (Tomskii) and the opening date of 8 May 1967.
entries.limitation: A commemorative institutional text.

entries.author: Piskaryovskoe Memorial Cemetery (museum website)
entries.title: Vechnyi ogon
entries.title_en: The Eternal Flame
entries.supports: The eternal flame on the Field of Mars (1957) and at Piskaryovskoe (1960), the relay of the flame, and the memorial’s opening in 1960.
entries.limitation: A museum information page; the claim of the first state-level flame is the museum’s own.

entries.author: The Russian Museum (virtual branch)
entries.title: Virtual exhibition: The Great Patriotic War
entries.supports: The designers and opening date of the Piskaryovskoe memorial (Vasil’ev, Levinson; 9 May 1960) and the contested totals of the buried.
entries.limitation: Museum text; the two totals (about 470,000 and about 520,000) are both reported there.

entries.author: Etkind, Alexander
entries.title: Warped Mourning: Stories of the Undead in the Land of the Unburied
entries.supports: The argument that Soviet culture was shaped by improperly buried dead and that Russian literature returns to them as the undead.
entries.limitation: A cultural-historical argument, presented here as interpretation.

entries.author: Tumarkin, Nina
entries.title: The Living and the Dead: The Rise and Fall of the Cult of World War II in Russia
entries.supports: The development of the Soviet cult of the Second World War and its memorial practices.
entries.limitation: The book was written before the post-Soviet memorial boom; used for the Soviet period only.

entries.author: State Tretyakov Gallery
entries.title: Vasilii Perov, ‘Provody pokoinika’, 1865 (collection record)
entries.supports: Title, date, dimensions (45.3 × 57 cm), inventory number (inv. 5248), provenance (Rumiantsev Museum, Soldatenkov collection), and the connection drawn to Nekrasov’s poem.
entries.limitation: A museum collection note, read through a search excerpt of the page (inventory number, size, provenance and the sentence on Nekrasov’s poem are in that excerpt); the plate’s description of the picture is from the painting itself.

entries.author: Moskovskaia pravda
entries.title: Ognennoe pogrebenie
entries.title_en: Burial by fire
entries.supports: Nothing is currently supported by this entry.
entries.limitation: DEAD LINK. On 2026-11-16 the URL returned an unrelated article (a 2025 concert notice), so the statements formerly attributed to it (1925 Moscow Soviet decision, 12 January 1927, German furnace) were not verified here and were re-sourced on plate K. Kept for the record only.

entries.author: Moskovskii komsomolets
entries.title: Na vystavke v Moskve pokazali put’ Malevicha
entries.title_en: An exhibition in Moscow traced Malevich’s path
entries.supports: That the artist was buried under a lone oak in the ‘Romashkovo field’; that the cube is described as in the form of a black square, a replacement cube of 1988 having a red square; that the oak was felled to sow the field, the grave was lost and the cube vanished.
entries.limitation: A newspaper feature, not a scholarly account of the grave. It places the cremation at the Danilov Monastery, which differs from Novaya Gazeta (Donskoy crematorium); the plate follows the latter. Read through a web-fetch summary of the page (machine summary).

entries.author: Yurchak, Alexei
entries.title: Everything Was Forever, Until It Was No More: The Last Soviet Generation
entries.supports: The late-Soviet relationship between official ritual language and everyday life; used as background for plate K.
entries.limitation: Not a study of funerary practice; cited for the general argument about official ritual.

entries.author: Lewkijewskaja, Jelena (Levkievskaia, E. E.); transl. Irina Lappo
entries.title: Semantyka okna w tradycyjnej kulturze Słowian Wschodnich
entries.title_en: The Semantics of the Window in the Traditional Culture of Eastern Slavs
entries.supports: The window as a ritual entrance and exit between this world and the other; souls and mythological figures pass through it in funeral rites and death legends; a house without windows as the dwelling of an alien being.
entries.limitation: Only the published abstract was read. The study generalises across the Eastern Slavs and is five pages long; it is a framing argument, not a regional record.

entries.author: Andryunina, Maria A.
entries.title: Anthropomorphic Symbolism of House in Funeral and Remembrance Rites: The Body, the Soul and the Sacrifice (Ukrainian, Belorusian, Western-Russian and Polish Traditions)
entries.supports: Doors and windows opened and holes made in the roof or ceiling at a death; the house regarded as broken afterwards and open to the unsettled soul; a new house regarded as incomplete until its first death.
entries.limitation: Year, issue and pages are not shown on the page and the record is incomplete. Only the abstract was read. The corpus is Ukrainian, Belarusian, western Russian and Polish, so it is not evidence for a single Russian custom.

entries.author: Plotnikova, Anna
entries.title: The Earthly Loci of Death: The Coffin, the Grave, the Cemetery
entries.publisher: Periodical not named on the PDF page read (Slovene-language publication, dlib.si)
entries.supports: The coffin, grave and graveyard as earthly forms of the home of the dead; the coffin built or furnished like a house; laments describing it as a cold dark house without windows; words for ‘coffin’ derived from ‘house’.
entries.limitation: Periodical title and year were not visible in the excerpt read, so the record is incomplete and should be completed before any claim rests on it. Covers Slavic traditions generally; regional attribution of individual details has not been traced.

entries.author: TASS (Itar-Tass)
entries.title: Russia’s population stands at 142,857,000 people, aged 39 on average (report on the official 2010 census results)
entries.supports: The 2010 census figure of 19,400 villages that exist de jure but have no inhabitants, 48 per cent more than at the previous census.
entries.limitation: A news agency’s report of the census report published in Rossiiskaya Gazeta. The Rosstat tables themselves were not consulted. ‘No inhabitants’ is a statistical status and says nothing about surviving buildings.

entries.author: Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW), Warsaw
entries.title: The results of the 2010 census – a deepening demographic crisis in Russia
entries.supports: The count of Russian villages falling by 8,500 over eight years to 134,000; rural population figures for 2002 and 2010.
entries.limitation: A think-tank analysis of Rosstat data, not the data itself; the analysis itself notes reservations about the census.

entries.author: RTE (Raidió Teilifís Éireann), news report
entries.title: Towns, villages a dying phenomenon in Russia
entries.supports: Rosstat head Alexander Surinov’s preliminary figures: villages with no population grown from 13,000 to 19,400; 36,200 villages with fewer than ten residents.
entries.limitation: Preliminary figures reported secondhand, published before the final census report; compare the TASS and OSW records.

entries.author: Kõiva, Mare; Boganeva, Elena; Butov, Ilya
entries.title: Forest Spirits and Their Functions in the Traditions of Estonians, Estonian Russians and Belarusians
entries.supports: That a path to the realm of the dead through the forest is a widespread rural belief, which the authors cite from Ivanov (1992) and do not claim as their own finding; the forest as a place of hostile forces or of hell.
entries.limitation: Only the passage on the path to the realm of the dead and the corpus description were read. The material is Estonian, Estonian-Russian and Belarusian; the Russian sample is about 108 archive texts against some 3,500 Estonian ones. It is not evidence for Russia as a whole.

entries.author: Santos Marinas, Enrique
entries.title: Myth and Immortality in Russian Folktales
entries.supports: An interpretation that the hut of Baba-Yaga, set at the edge of the forest or in a clearing, marks a threshold to the Other World, with its owner as guardian of that passage.
entries.limitation: Only the abstract and the passage on the hut’s location were read. The corpus is Afanasyev’s published folktales, so this is a reading of narrative, not a record of burial or belief practice.

entries.author: Lavrenova, Olga
entries.title: On the Borderline of the Worlds: Swamps in the Mythopoetic World Picture of the Peoples of Russia
entries.publisher: Shima: The International Journal of Research into Island Cultures 16(2)
entries.supports: Swamps treated as a liminal space between water and land and between worlds; accounts of swamps as places the dead go and of swamp spirits that drag people down, including kikimoras described as girls drowned in a swamp.
entries.limitation: An interpretive essay built on secondary sources (folklore collections, dictionaries, scholarly summaries) with no stated sampling method, so its examples are illustrative, not representative. It covers many peoples, among them Russians, Komi, Khanty, Tungus and Yakut, so a given example is not automatically Russian. It says little about burial.

entries.author: Bolshaya rossiiskaya entsiklopediya (online edition), unsigned entry
entries.title: Семик
entries.title_en: Semik
entries.supports: Semik as a time to remember people who died without repentance or burial, among them the drowned; a Vyatka day dedicated to the drowned; a Smolensk ban on washing and water work at Semik so that no one in the family would drown; wreaths and birches thrown into rivers; communal pits (skudelnitsy) for unidentified bodies until Semik, and an 1771 ban on burial in them.
entries.limitation: The page shows no author, year or volume, so the entry cannot be fully cited; it names regional examples without giving their original records. Read through a summary of the page, not line by line. Re-checked 2026-11-16 through a web-fetch summary of the page (machine summary): Semik as the Thursday before Trinity; the Vyatka drowned’s day with boisterous memorial meals; the Smolensk water ban; wreaths and birches in water; skudelnitsy and the decree of Catherine II of 25 March (5 April) 1771 all stated; the entry is neither signed nor dated.

entries.author: Krinichnaya, N. A.
entries.title: На росстани: мифологема судьбы в фольклорно-этнографическом освещении
entries.title_en: At the Crossroads: The Mythologeme of Fate in Folkloristic and Ethnographic Perspective
entries.supports: The crossroads (rosstan) as the usual place to see off travellers and wait for returning kin, a custom of parting at the village edge; the author’s reconstruction that burial at crossroads goes back to ancestor cults and was later applied to those who died ‘unnaturally’.
entries.limitation: Parting and funeral practice are secondary to the article’s subject, fate, and are treated briefly. The reconstruction rests on fragmentary, often 19th-century records and on the idea of survivals, so much of it is hypothesis. The material is mostly North Russian (Karelia, Onega region, Vologda, Kostroma), with thin Ukrainian and Belarusian evidence, and it gives no figures on how widespread any practice was. Stage 2: the burial passage, the Primary Chronicle quotation and notes 45–49 were re-read in the owner’s PDF; the rest of the article was not read line by line.

entries.author: Matlin, M. G.
entries.title: Смерть в ландшафте: пространственный аспект современной традиции отмечать места гибели людей на автодорогах (на примере российских федеральных трасс А 151, Р 178, Р 241)
entries.title_en: Death in the Landscape: A Spatial Aspect of the Modern Tradition of Marking Places of Death on Highways (Federal Highways A 151, R 178, R 241)
entries.supports: A continuous field survey of roadside memorial signs on three Middle Volga highway sections totalling 362 km (A 151 Chuvashia 120 km, R 241 Tatarstan 130 km, R 178 Mordovia 112 km), visited between July 2013 and April 2021: 299 signs (132, 95 and 72), each photographed and located, dated 1965–2019; two families of sign, one imitating cemetery forms and one not; differences in placement by region (largest shares: slope 47.9% in Mordovia, roadside strip 30.8% in Tatarstan, woodland or forest belt about 62% in Chuvashia); temporary items (flowers, wreaths, ribbons, toys) distinguished from permanent ones (wood, metal, stone).
entries.limitation: Three routes in three neighbouring republics, so the findings may not hold elsewhere. The lifespan of temporary items could not be established (ten signs were seen to last one to three years); density figures overstate what a driver sees and the article reports only high-density stretches; the claim that drivers read the road as a cemetery rests on comments and density, not on measurement. Coordinates were determined for some signs (Yandex and Google maps); no per-sign list is published. The author photographed the signs and partly interviewed road workers and residents (number not given). The signs mark road deaths of 1965–2019, not the older customs on this plate. Full text read through a summary of the PDF at press.psu.ru (re-checked 2026-11-16: lengths, counts, date ranges, visit years, sign families, placement shares, ten signs lasting one to three years), not line by line.

entries.author: Filatova, E. A.
entries.title: Градостроительная ревитализация затопленных территорий Верхнего Поволжья
entries.title_en: Urban Planning Revitalization of Flooded Territories of the Upper Volga Region
entries.supports: Context figures for the Rybinsk and Uglich reservoirs: more than 300,000 hectares flooded, more than 40 churches, three monasteries, about 700 villages and hamlets, and six towns including Mologa and Korcheva.
entries.limitation: A planning proposal to lower the reservoir level and restore settlements, so it argues a case. The figures are given without a primary citation in the part read, and the text gives no figures for graves or cemeteries. Read through a summary of the article, not line by line. The introduction’s figures (over 300,000 ha; over 40 churches; three monasteries; about 700 villages; six towns including Mologa and Korcheva) were re-checked on 2026-11-16 in the article’s text at academvestnik.ru (search excerpt).

entries.author: Tsipileva, I.
entries.title: О переселении жителей Череповецкого района из зоны затопления в связи с образованием Рыбинского водохранилища
entries.title_en: On the Resettlement of Residents of Cherepovets District from the Flood Zone During the Creation of the Rybinsk Reservoir
entries.publisher: Vologda Regional Universal Research Library, web edition (© 2014)
entries.supports: That resettlement followed a decree of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee and the Council of People’s Commissars of 1 August 1936, and that the residents of about seven hundred villages and hamlets were moved out of the flood zone.
entries.limitation: Only the opening of the article was seen, through a search excerpt; the year of first publication is not shown. The article’s own focus is one district.

entries.author: RAPSI (rapsinews.ru); no author named on the page
entries.title: Русская Атлантида: право затопленных городов
entries.title_en: Russian Atlantis: the law of flooded cities
entries.supports: A claim, to be checked, that the sanitary preparation of the reservoir bed called for moving cemeteries but only some churchyards were moved in the 1930s–40s, so many Mologa-area cemeteries went under water; and that estimates of the number resettled range from 100,000 to 130,000, with historians disputing how they were counted.
entries.limitation: Page read in full on 2026-11-16 through a machine summary of the page (published 13 July 2026, modified 17 July). It states the claims in this entry but names no archive, decree, historian or document for the cemetery claim or for the 100,000–130,000 range; it names other decrees (no. 2074 of 14 September 1935; no. 668 of 5 May 1940; RSFSR Presidium, 20 December 1940) and gives 13 April 1941 as the start of filling. A news feature: treat every claim from it as unverified until a primary record is found.

entries.author: Azbyka.ru (Orthodox pilgrim reference)
entries.title: Псково-Печерский монастырь (пещеры)
entries.title_en: Pskov-Caves Monastery (the caves)
entries.supports: The far caves called the monastery cemetery; the caves first used only to bury monks, with laypeople later (the first recorded in 1528; monks in the fifth and sixth of seven galleries); the total number of burials given as about ten thousand.
entries.limitation: A devotional pilgrim reference with no archive, register or author named for the figure. Re-read on 2026-11-16 through a web-fetch summary of the full page (machine summary): ‘monastery cemetery’ is said of the far caves, not the near caves (which the page describes as short P-shaped passages with the relics of four saints); the 10,000 figure is for the whole burial complex. The figure is a reported total, not a count.

entries.author: Anokhin, D.
entries.title: Разгадки подземелий: мюоны помогли найти потайные помещения в монастырских подвалах
entries.title_en: Solving the underground: muons helped find hidden rooms in the monastery cellars
entries.publisher: Strana Rosatom, 19 October 2023 (copy in the MEPhI open repository)
entries.supports: A popular account of the 2023 muon survey of two blind ends in the Pskov-Caves Monastery: a hidden passage about 12 m long behind a walled crypt, a continuation of Trinity Street beyond the barrier, and an unknown cavity of roughly 3 × 6 × 3 m. Seven accessible underground streets over 200 m in all; more than 10,000 burials reported. Legends of tunnels to Izborsk presented as unverified folklore.
entries.limitation: A newspaper feature, not the scientific paper. Re-read on 2026-11-16 through a web-fetch summary (machine summary): author Dmitry Anokhin; the team is led by Natalya Polukhina (no patronymic given); the dimensions are given as reported by the team; the over 10,000 burials are stated without a register; nuclear emulsions are mentioned only in a sidebar; the Izborsk tunnel account (about 15 km) is attributed to Metropolitan Tikhon, head of the monastery, and presented as legends.

entries.author: Alexandrov, A. B., et al. (23 authors, among them N. G. Polukhina)
entries.title: Muography of the Cave Church of the Holy Dormition Pskovo-Pechersky Monastery
entries.publisher: Bulletin of the Lebedev Physics Institute, vol. 50, no. 12
entries.supports: That a muographic study with nuclear emulsion detectors was made of two objects in the cave complex of the monastery, and that the method images the internal structure of objects from the tracks of atmospheric muons.
entries.limitation: Only the abstract and bibliographic data of the journal version were read. For dimensions and method the plate uses the open preprint (alexandrov2023-preprint) and the popular account.

entries.author: Kuzmitsky, Vadim (Delovoi Peterburg)
entries.title: Православная Европа: как продвигается реставрация Псково–Печерского монастыря
entries.title_en: Orthodox Europe: how the restoration of the Pskov-Caves Monastery is going
entries.supports: That a local legend runs the caves from Pechory to Izborsk, about 20 km; that the caves were used for mass burials; that the head of a restoration firm reports 486 keramidy (tomb-closing slabs) found, the earliest from the 15th century.
entries.limitation: A business newspaper, re-read on 2026-11-16 through a web-fetch summary of the first 100,000 characters of the page (machine summary). It gives about 20 km for the legend where the Rosatom feature says about 15 km, so the distance is not settled by either. The legend is not evidence of a tunnel. The 486 is a count of slabs, quoted from a firm’s head, not of burials.

entries.author: Rouhier-Willoughby, Jeanmarie
entries.title: Contemporary Urban Russian Funerals: Continuity and Change
entries.supports: For the traditional village, citing Zelenin, Baiburin, Kabakova, Kremleva and Sedakova: all mirrors covered at a death, all water in the house thrown out, the body laid for three days on the table under the icon corner with the head beneath the icons. For Soviet urban practice, shiny surfaces covered. It also records the coffin leaving by a back door or window at burial.
entries.limitation: A review that draws on earlier ethnographers and on interviews about urban practice, so the village customs come at second hand. It does not mention opening a window at death or stopping clocks. Read in an automated extract, not in the original pages.

entries.author: Ansimova, O. K.; Golubkova, O. V.
entries.title: Mythological Characters of the Domestic Space in Russian Folk Beliefs: Lexicographic and Ethnographic Aspects
entries.publisher: Archaeology, Ethnology and Anthropology of Eurasia, vol. 44, no. 3
entries.supports: The domovoy described as a home spirit and generic ancestor, citing Krinichnaya (2004) for the ancestor's soul that became the soul of the house; field materials of 1999–2015 from the Novosibirsk, Omsk, Tyumen, Leningrad, Pskov, Novgorod, Vologda, Kirov and Altai regions; offerings of food; the domovoy as a possible restless soul of a relative that may knock before a death; the bannik and obderikha set apart as the most dangerous; the kikimora linked to unbaptised dead infants, not to ancestors.
entries.limitation: No archives named and no count of field records. The 2015 questionnaire had 317 urban respondents (Novosibirsk 37%, Moscow 22%, St Petersburg 17%, others less) and did not show the ancestor-soul belief; the article calls students aged 17–25 the main part, but its own breakdown gives 21% students and 53% with higher education. The forty-day detail comes from one Novosibirsk informant and the commemoration food from one Pskov informant. Some rural material is recollection (kikimora mummers of the 1950s in places in Western Siberia). The ancestor reading is cited to Krinichnaya 2004 (pp. 150–155, 175), not shown here. Re-checked 2026-11-16 against the open full text (journal.archaeology.nsc.ru) through machine summaries.

entries.author: Granova, M. A.
entries.title: Мифологическая традиция поселка Северный Коммунар Сивинского района Пермского края: представления о домовом
entries.title_en: Mythological Tradition of the Settlement of Severny Kommunar, Sivinsky District, Perm Krai: Ideas about the Domovoy
entries.publisher: Vestnik Permskogo universiteta. Rossiiskaia i zarubezhnaia filologiia, vol. 11, no. 3
entries.supports: One village’s domovoy beliefs recorded in June 2019: names such as domovoy and dedushka-domovoy, read as possibly pointing to a family ancestor; forms (a small hairy old man, a cat, a weasel; visible only to small children and animals); sweets left for him and the table not left empty overnight (formulas for taking him to a new house are cited from other districts only); a belief in a second, harmful female spirit in the cellar; and a marked reduction of the beliefs, with media influence.
entries.limitation: One village; the number of informants and records is not stated. The ancestor link is offered as a possibility in the names (dedushka may also describe an old man’s look), not as a statement by informants. The media and reduction conclusions are given as tendencies (the cartoon origin of Kuzka is a suggestion with an alternative derivation). Re-checked 2026-11-16 against the open full text (press.psu.ru) through a machine summary: volume 11, issue 3, pp. 27–37.

entries.author: Culture.ru (state cultural portal), author not shown
entries.title: Какие духи дома почитались на Руси?
entries.title_en: Which house spirits were venerated in Rus?
entries.supports: Only as a lead: the page, citing the academician N. I. Tolstoy, says it was a custom to build a house where an ancestor’s remains lay, and sometimes to bury the first member of the family to die after the housewarming under the threshold.
entries.limitation: A popular portal read in a search excerpt; the passage is not traced to a page of Tolstoy’s book, and no region or period is given. It is not used to support any statement on the plate.

entries.author: Ovseichik, V. E. (Auseichyk, U.)
entries.title: «Нечистые» покойники в представлениях населения белорусско-русского (Полоцко-Псковского и Витебско-Смоленского) пограничья
entries.title_en: ‘Impure’ dead in the perceptions of the population of the Belarusian-Russian (Polotsk-Pskov and Vitebsk-Smolensk) borderland
entries.supports: Categories of ‘impure’ dead in the Vitebsk, Pskov and Smolensk border region (unbaptised children, suicides, sorcerers); burial of suicides and sorcerers away from the common cemetery in the 19th and early 20th centuries; the reported measures against sorcerers (stake, severed head); Zelenin’s 1916 term ‘zalozhnye’ from Vyatka dialect and the author’s refusal to extend it to the whole category; walking dead rare in East Slavic material.
entries.limitation: Number of informants and records is not stated for any category (checked for the sorcerer measures in particular). Archive records (folklore archives of Polotsk and Pskov State Universities, said to be largely unpublished), published collections, 19th-century publications (Nikiforovsky, Dobrovolsky, Bogdanovich) and the author’s own notes are not always told apart; the walking and blood-drinking accounts are from the 19th–early 20th-century sources. Other categories, such as women who died in childbirth, are said to be too scattered to reconstruct. Re-read 2026-11-16 in a machine summary of the open PDF (ojs.zrc-sazu.si), not page by page; a DOI link is blocked here.

entries.author: Ryko, A.
entries.title: Funeral Rites in the Russian-Belarusian Borderland: Traditions and Innovations
entries.publisher: Chinese Journal of Slavic Studies, vol. 5, no. 1
entries.supports: Khislavichi district, Smolensk region, fieldwork 2018–2019: a former ban on burying those who hanged or drowned themselves in the common cemetery, remembered by informants born in the 1930s; younger people say the drowned lay in the common cemetery; unbaptised infants not treated as ‘unclean’; no one now says such dead return.
entries.limitation: Informant and record counts not stated. The author says data from different informants sometimes diverge and many informants cannot explain their actions, and that it is unclear whether the trend is isolated; answering needs wider comparative material. Re-read 2026-11-16 in the open HTML full text (degruyterbrill.com) through a machine summary, not page by page.

entries.author: Avdeev, A.
entries.title: Суеверия, погребальные обряды и древнерусская эпиграфика
entries.title_en: Superstitions, funeral ceremonies, and old Russian epigraphy
entries.publisher: Vestnik Pravoslavnogo Svyato-Tikhonovskogo gumanitarnogo universiteta, Seriya II, no. 86
entries.supports: Only the abstract: from 16th–early 18th-century epitaphs and letters of hierarchs, the author finds no obstacle to cemetery burial or regular commemoration of those who died violent ‘vain’ deaths, and argues the related superstitions are not pagan survivals but arose in Christian times.
entries.limitation: Abstract only; the article itself was not read, so its evidence and its limits are not checked here. The conclusion is one author’s and runs against the earlier ethnographic reading.

entries.author: Townsend, D. A.
entries.title: From Upyr' to Vampire: The Slavic Vampire Myth in Russian Literature
entries.supports: Only the abstract: the Slavic vampire myth traced to pre-Orthodox belief became a literary device in Russian writing from the 18th century onward.
entries.limitation: Abstract only; the thesis was not read. It is used for one statement, that the literary vampire is a later device, and for nothing about field belief.

entries.author: Hieromonk Job (Gumerov)
entries.title: Why are the Dead Commemorated on Saturdays?
entries.supports: The Church’s own account of its Saturdays of commemoration: Meat Fare Saturday, the second, third and fourth Saturdays of Great Lent, Trinity Saturday and St. Demetrius Saturday; the reasons given for Saturday; the origin given for Demetrius Saturday after the battle of Kulikovo (1380).
entries.limitation: A church instructional text, not a historical study: it states what the Church holds and gives its own dates of institution without footnotes. It says nothing of Radonitsa, Semik or village practice. Re-checked 2026-11-16 (machine summary of the English translation on OrthoChristian): author Hieromonk Job (Gumerov); the list of Saturdays and the Kulikovo origin confirmed.

entries.author: Maltsev, G. I.
entries.title: Поминки и поминовения умерших не своей смертью у коми-пермяков
entries.title_en: Permyak memorial rituals and commemorations of those who died an unnatural death among the Komi-Permyaks
entries.publisher: Finno-Ugric studies journal (Udmurt State University), vol. 14, no. 2
entries.supports: Commemoration days among the Komi-Permyaks (Radonitsa, Semik, Trinity Saturday, Pokrov and Dmitrievskaya Saturdays); the statement that Semik is absent from the Orthodox calendar, with priests absent from it in the late 19th century and present from the early 20th; the report, after Zelenin, that those dead by unnatural death were commemorated at Semik; a gradual move of that commemoration to funeral Saturdays. Also, from the same reading: the day is called dzollun or sharlun; the commemorated are mainly suicides, the drowned and those described as ‘poisoned’; it is held at the cemetery, where such dead were often buried at the edge, and suicides were also remembered at home with food set on a water barrel or the threshold; families bring pancakes, pies and bread; priests joined in the early 20th century and a memorial service is held today in the Kudymkar diocese; fieldwork in the Yusva, Gayny and Kosa districts (1995–2016) with Kungur and Komi Zyuzda published material.
entries.limitation: Komi-Permyak, not Russian material, and used only as a regional comparison. Four field recordings of the author (Yusva 2010 and 2016, Gayny 2005, Kosa 1995), plus other informants quoted without a total count. The journal title is not printed in the text read; the page is hosted at journals.udsu.ru/finno-ugric and year, volume, issue and pages (2020, 14(2), 279–283) come from the DOI. The printed Russian title is ‘Поминки и поминовения умерших не своей смертью у коми-пермяков’ (the ‘Пермяцкие’ variant was a mistake). The conclusion is hedged by the author. Re-read 2026-11-16 in the open PDF (journals.udsu.ru) through a machine summary; the DOI link is blocked here. The offerings listed in the article include reports from Uzhum and from other Permyak places, not only the districts of the author’s own fieldwork.

entries.author: Chesnokova, E. G.
entries.title: Cemetery in the Context of the Contemporary Calendar Holiday
entries.publisher: Traditional Culture (almanac), 2018, vol. 19, no. 1 (Institute of Ethnology and Anthropology RAS)
entries.supports: Fieldwork of 2016–2017 in the Kostroma and Vladimir regions: the main commemoration falls in the Easter or the Trinity period according to regional zones; one day of that period holds the main cemetery rites; the structure of that day; family and social character; a held or growing importance.
entries.limitation: Abstract read on the almanac’s page (2026-11-16, machine summary): author Elena G. Chesnokova, Institute of Ethnology and Anthropology RAS; Traditional Culture, 2018, vol. 19, no. 1. Pages and the text itself were not read. The day is not named in the abstract and the regional zones are not named either. Respondent and record counts are not given.

entries.author: Author not shown on the page read
entries.title: Восточнославянская похоронная обрядность
entries.title_en: East Slavic funeral rites
entries.supports: The two aims of the rite as the article states them (helping the dead reach the other world; protecting the living); cleansing and protective acts (washing the house after the coffin is carried out, turning objects over, covering mirrors, washing hands after the cemetery) and prohibitions (close relatives making the coffin, bringing food back from the cemetery); washing of the body as obligatory; regional variants (hired older women in the Russian North, spruce branches in Arkhangelsk).
entries.limitation: No author, date or edition on the page that was read, so it is cited as an anonymous encyclopedia article. It states an explanation in general (the dead can harm the living; the boundary stays open until burial and the fortieth day) and gives none for each act. It does not date its examples. The page has no bibliography; the authorities it names in the text are Baiburin 1993 (pp. 101, 107–108, 119), Razumova 2012 (p. 44), Tolstaya, ‘Pominki’ 2009 (p. 162), Tolstaya 2019 (pp. 295–297), Spassky 1877 no. 18 (p. 604) and ‘Materialy dlya izucheniya byta…’ 1890 (p. 521), without publication details. None of them was opened.

entries.author: Hieromonk Dometian
entries.title: Православие против суеверий
entries.title_en: Orthodoxy against superstition
entries.supports: The Church’s polemical position: covering mirrors in a house of mourning is called a folk custom unrelated to the Orthodox burial rite; the reasons the author reports for it (the soul should not be frightened by its reflection; the dead should not frighten the family; a fear of the soul going into the mirror); belief that one must not look out of a window at a funeral procession; turning tables and chairs over called a pagan survival.
entries.limitation: A church polemical text; it reports popular reasons in order to condemn them, so its account of belief is filtered. No publisher or year of first publication on the page read. It is evidence of the Church’s stance and of customs it names, not a study.

entries.author: Radio Svoboda interview with E. Krasilnikova (interviewer not named)
entries.title: Как и почему большевики сносили старые кладбища
entries.title_en: How and why the Bolsheviks demolished old cemeteries
entries.supports: The interviewee’s account (E. Krasilnikova, professor at Novosibirsk State Technical University, author of a book on the subject) of cemetery demolition in Siberia from the mid-1920s: dated decisions in Novosibirsk (1920 on the cemetery grove, 1929 on closing the Voskresenskaya church, an April 1930 protest of about 1,000 people dispersed by the militia); the old cemetery becoming a garden and later a park; two large cemeteries destroyed in Barnaul in the 1930s; the Omsk necropolis surviving until the 1950s, recorded by a museum director, with fragments gathered into a memorial square in 2005.
entries.limitation: A newspaper interview. The dated decisions are given as facts but no archive or file is cited; the motives (ideology, neglect after the Civil War, symbolism, mobilising funerals) and the claim that Barnaul was the most radical case are the interviewee’s interpretation. Siberian material only; the book it draws on was not read.

entries.author: Minkin, A.
entries.title: Надгробия под ногами
entries.title_en: Gravestones Underfoot
entries.supports: A 2019 report of gravestones found used as curbs near the Estrada Theatre on Bersenevskaya Embankment in Moscow, with photos posted by a municipal deputy; the construction department’s statement that the work was not its own; an earlier case of 2011; and statements by an architect (S. Tkachenko) and by the state enterprise ‘Ritual’ about reuse of stone in the 1920s–30s.
entries.limitation: Journalism. The historical claims (reuse of granite in the 1920s–30s, rubble from 1934 demolitions used as metro filler, cemeteries cleared for the metro and roads, slabs crushed into rubble) are statements by an expert and an agency, and no document or archive is cited for them. The 2019 curbs are shown through a deputy’s social-media photos.

entries.author: Sergeeva, A.; Gerlit, R.; Krcmar, H.
entries.title: Digital inheritance in Russia
entries.supports: Only the abstract: an analysis of 33 social networks and online services, a survey of 173 internet users and expert interviews; the authors expect services to host more dead than living users in coming decades, accounts and data to persist, the deceased to keep receiving invitations and greetings, and heirs to find it hard to identify accounts and reach data.
entries.limitation: Abstract only; the article was not read, so the survey sample and its limits are not known here. The ‘more dead than living’ line is an expectation, not a count.

entries.author: Linden, K.
entries.title: Death Online in Contemporary Russia: Memory, Forgetting and the Connective Presence of Mourning on the Internet
entries.supports: Only the library abstract: virtual ethnography of three memorial websites (on Soviet repressions, on the Nord-Ost siege, and on social networking sites); the argument that online tools enable communal remembrance, that digitalisation may challenge Russia’s political memory culture, and that the ‘right to be forgotten’ is not necessarily the answer.
entries.limitation: Abstract only; year not shown on the page read, and the full text (linked there) was not read. The claims are the author’s argument in a theoretical framework (existential media studies), not findings that were checked here.

entries.author: HSE University news service, reporting T. Khusyainov and E. Urusova
entries.title: Hi-Tech Grief: HSE Researchers Explore the Pros and Cons of Digital Commemoration
entries.publisher: HSE University (hse.ru), 27 March 2025; the underlying article is in the journal Chelovek
entries.supports: The researchers’ claims as relayed by a university news item: digital footprints and virtual memorials; AI avatars of the dead that recreate voice and habits and can contain errors; a possible support for grief by sustained connection and a possible delay of acceptance and retraumatisation; platforms as de facto data owners.
entries.limitation: A news item, not the article; the article itself and its title were not read. The item does not discuss Russia’s own law. Claims about grief are the researchers’ claims.

entries.author: Skorodumova-Cheglokova, R. P.
entries.title: Все понимали, что переезд неизбежен
entries.title_en: Everyone understood that the move was unavoidable
entries.publisher: Web edition of a local-history collection, Vologda Regional Universal Research Library (booksite.ru, section «mariinka»)
entries.supports: A resettled woman's recollection that, before the flooding of the Rybinsk reservoir, even recent cemetery burials were offered for transfer to anyone who wished it (to Topornya or elsewhere).
entries.limitation: Read only in a search excerpt; the page itself could not be fetched, so the village, the year and the collection's title and date were not confirmed. One person's memory, not an official record; it shows that transfer was offered on request, not how many graves were moved or whether the offer was general.

entries.author: Matlin, M. G.
entries.title: Personalization and Anonymization of the Place of Death of a Person in an Accident (Using the Example of Federal Highways A 151, P 178, P 241) — Russian title not captured
entries.title_en: Personalization and Anonymization of the Place of Death of a Person in an Accident (Using the Example of Federal Highways A 151, P 178, P 241)
entries.supports: From the abstract: signs that give no information about the dead make up 19% of all signs on R 241, 33% on A 151 and 50% on R 178; the author links the higher shares to flowerpots, gazebos and fences without plates, and to old metal signs that have lost photographs and plates.
entries.limitation: Abstract only (DOAJ record); the article was not read. The percentages and the explanation are the author's, and the abstract does not give counts. The 33% (A 151) and 50% (R 178) figures were seen again in the article’s own text excerpt on 2026-11-16.

entries.author: Alexandrov, A., et al. (23 authors, among them N. Polukhina)
entries.title: Muonography of Caves of the Holy Dormition Pskovo-Pechersky Monastery
entries.publisher: Preprints.org, v1, posted 13 September 2023 (not peer-reviewed; CC BY 4.0)
entries.supports: Method and results of the 2023 muon survey: 13 nuclear-emulsion detectors (two in the Assumption Church attic for background, eleven underground), exposed 112 days; two objects. A crypt behind a large icon at the cave entrance, about 2.5 × 2.5 m, with a corridor 1–3 m wide and up to 12 m long perpendicular to Main Street; a cavity at Trinity Street about 2 m high and roughly 3 × 6 m, at 77–79 m altitude, and the street continuing along its direction. No formal error margins; dimensions are rough estimates. The paper gives no number of burials and says only that the caves were used as a necropolis from the monastery's founding.
entries.limitation: An earlier, non-peer-reviewed version of the journal paper (the published title differs). Read through a summary of the preprint page, not line by line; the figures themselves were not inspected. Re-read on 2026-11-16 through a web-fetch summary of the preprint page: 13 detectors, 112 days, crypt about 2.5 × 2.5 m, corridor 1–3 m by up to 12 m, cavity about 2 m high and about 3 × 6 m, altitude 77–79 m, no formal uncertainties, no count of burials, seven galleries over 200 m at depths of 3–15 m; confirmed.

entries.author: Azbyka.ru news desk (unsigned)
entries.title: В России православные отмечают Радоницу
entries.title_en: In Russia Orthodox Christians mark Radonitsa
entries.supports: The Church’s present rule that Radonitsa always falls on the ninth day after Easter, the Tuesday of Thomas week, and falls on 14 May in 2024; the reasons given from the typikon for placing it there.
entries.limitation: A church news item read in a search excerpt, not in full; it states the Church’s current rule, not older or local practice.

entries.author: Soikin, P. P. (publisher); entry unsigned
entries.title: Радоница (in: Полный православный богословский энциклопедический словарь)
entries.title_en: Radonitsa (in: Complete Orthodox Theological Encyclopaedic Dictionary)
entries.publisher: P. P. Soikin, St Petersburg, vol. 2
entries.supports: Radonitsa as a day of commemoration of the dead falling mostly on the Monday, and in some places on the Tuesday, of the week after Easter week, called Thomas week.
entries.limitation: A short unsigned entry in a pre-revolutionary reference work, read in a transcription on Azbyka.ru; it gives the variation but names no places. Re-checked 2026-11-16: the visible text is the opening paragraph only; the entry says ‘usually Monday’, Tuesday in some localities; it is unsigned (Soikin, 1913, vol. 2).

entries.author: BFM.ru news desk (unsigned in the excerpt)
entries.title: Москвичи поднимались в Театр эстрады по могильным плитам
entries.title_en: Muscovites climbed to the Estrada Theatre over gravestones
entries.supports: That fragments of gravestones with 18th- and 19th-century dates were found at the Estrada Theatre on Bersenevskaya Embankment, described as granite steps taken up for repair; that A. Frolov of the Arkhnadzor council attributed one slab to the gravestone of Colonel Pyotr Beketov from the Novospassky Monastery and read the find as a trace of 1930s clearing of old cemeteries.
entries.limitation: A news item read in a search excerpt. The attribution of the slab is one preservationist’s statement, not an inspection record. It describes steps where the 360.ru report (minkin2019) describes curbs, so the two reports differ on what the stones were used as.

entries.author: RTVI news desk, citing TASS and the VK press service
entries.title: «ВКонтакте» начала помечать страницы умерших пользователей по просьбе их родственников
entries.title_en: VKontakte has begun marking pages of dead users at their relatives’ request
entries.publisher: RTVI, 26 November (year not shown in the excerpt read)
entries.supports: That VK marks or deletes the page of a dead user at relatives’ request on a photograph of the death certificate, the mark ‘Страница умершего человека’ replacing the last-visit time; that since 2011 a page could be kept unchanged or deleted; and, for other services, a black ribbon or black-and-white photo on Odnoklassniki and a ‘legacy contact’ with a memorial label on Facebook.
entries.limitation: A news item read in a search excerpt; the year is not shown. It reports a platform policy as of its date. Platform rules change, and the platforms’ own help pages were not read.

entries.author: Drannikova, N. V.
entries.title: Домашние духи-«хозяева» в севернорусском и норвежском фольклоре (типологические аспекты)
entries.title_en: Domestic ‘master’ spirits in North Russian and Norwegian folklore: typological aspects
entries.publisher: Collection or journal not named on the PDF page read (Northern (Arctic) Federal University, Arkhangelsk)
entries.supports: For Arkhangelsk Oblast: about 23 names of the domovoy; that he is usually considered a deceased family member and first ancestor of the clan, in one formulation a man who died unrepentant; that he may look like a dead grandfather; his appearance (anthropomorphic, animal, or known only by sounds); the prediction of good or ill while he ‘presses’ a sleeper, bad omens (groaning, knocking) often foreshadowing a death in the family; the ritual invitation when moving house.
entries.limitation: Journal or collection, year and issue are not shown on the page read, so the record is incomplete. Field material from the author’s expeditions to Arkhangelsk districts in 1990–2012 and earlier collections (Maksimov, Zelenin), with no count of records; a typological article, with the Norwegian comparison left aside. Read in a machine summary of the PDF, not line by line. Re-checked 2026-11-16 (machine summary of the PDF): ancestor and first-ancestor statements, 23 names, knock and groan before a death, and the 1990–2012 expeditions confirmed; the resemblance to a dead grandfather is an example, not a stated rule.

entries.author: Denisevich, K. N. (student, RGGU)
entries.title: Домовой и домашний скот в поверьях Каргополья
entries.title_en: The domovoy and domestic livestock in Kargopol beliefs
entries.publisher: Collection not named on the PDF page read; section ‘Beliefs and rites’, RGGU ethnolinguistic expedition materials
entries.supports: For the Kargopol area (Arkhangelsk Oblast): the domovoy as a helpful ‘master’ of the household who looks like the head of the family and cares for livestock; names such as khozyain and the euphemisms zapechnik and podpolnik; the baennik of the bathhouse, the ovinnik of the threshing barn and the dvorovoy of the yard as separate spirits; and the author’s statement that the domovoy is closely tied to the ancestor cult although the text does not say he is a dead person.
entries.limitation: A short piece by a student, from the expedition of the Russian State University for the Humanities; the years of the expeditions, the collection and the year of publication are not given on the page read. The relation to the dead is a general statement of the author, not an informant’s report. Read in a machine summary of the PDF. Re-checked 2026-11-16 (machine summary): the author is Ksenia N. Denisevich of RGGU; the ancestor link is discussed for the domovoy only; the dvorovoy is treated as not wholly separate from him.

entries.author: Neskuchny Sad (journal), expert: Archpriest Boris Levshenko
entries.title: Mytarstva: bogoslovskoe modelirovanie (Toll-houses: theological modelling)
entries.supports: The Life of St Basil the New as source of the Theodora vision (10th c., Constantinople, per the Orthodox Encyclopedia as cited there); the statement that the toll-house narrative never became binding dogma.
entries.limitation: A popular theological article; not a primary text of the Life.

entries.author: Azbyka.ru editors
entries.title: Roditelskie subboty (Parental Saturdays)
entries.supports: Rule that 3rd/9th/40th-day commemorations falling in Great Lent are moved to the nearest Saturday; church rules do not regulate the memorial meal.
entries.limitation: Reference page without a named author.

entries.author: Loiter, S. M.
entries.title: Irina Fedosova v issledovaniyakh K. V. Chistova (Irina Fedosova in the work of K. V. Chistov)
entries.publisher: Uchenye zapiski Petrozavodskogo gosudarstvennogo universiteta, no. 1 (162), pp. 61–66
entries.supports: Fedosova (1827–1899), lamenter of the Zaonezhye; Chistov’s long study of her; Agreneva-Slavianskaia’s additional recordings.
entries.limitation: Abstract and excerpts read; dates differ in some reference works (1827 vs 1831).

entries.author: Mertsalova, A.
entries.title: 12 мест в Москве, на которых раньше были кладбища
entries.title_en: 12 places in Moscow where cemeteries used to be
entries.supports: A newspaper list of Moscow cemeteries liquidated in the 20th century, with the year of the decision, what stands on the site now and, for some, whether graves were moved (Dorogomilovskoe, Simonov Monastery, Lazarevskoe, Mazilovskoe, Bratskoe and others).
entries.limitation: Journalism, read in full through a web-fetch summary (machine summary) on 2026-11-16: the six rows on plate L match it. No archive or file is cited for any decision or date; relocation is stated for some entries and left unstated for others, which does not mean nothing was moved. ‘Now’ descriptions are as of 2013.

entries.author: Sokolova, A. D.
entries.title: Крематорий-храм, или кремация в советском похоронном обряде 1920-х годов
entries.title_en: Crematorium-Temple, or Cremation in the Soviet Funeral Rite of the 1920s
entries.supports: Cremation in the USSR as a civil authorities’ decision driven by sanitation; the first project (Petrograd) framed as a ‘Crematorium-Temple’ meant to create a needed spiritual mood; by the second half of the 1920s, when the Donskoy crematorium was built, the attitude to cremation as technology outweighed the quasi-religious framing.
entries.limitation: Abstract and opening paragraphs read; the article’s archival detail was not read.

entries.author: Guinness World Records
entries.title: Largest crematorium
entries.supports: Nikolo-Arkhangelsk Crematorium, east Moscow, completed March 1972: seven twin cremators and six halls of farewell, as the record entry describes it.
entries.limitation: A records entry, not a history; it gives no source for the figures.

entries.author: coldwarsites.net (editor not named)
entries.title: Donskoy Cemetery and Crematorium, Moscow
entries.supports: The page’s statement that the Donskoy crematorium, built in 1927, was closed in 1973 and rebuilt as a church in 1990.
entries.limitation: A hobbyist site with no citations. Other pages read say the Donskoy crematorium was the only one in Moscow until the mid-1970s; the closing date is therefore unconfirmed.

entries.author: Smirnov, K.
entries.title: Казимир Малевич: сенсации 2015 года
entries.title_en: Kazimir Malevich: the sensations of 2015
entries.supports: Account of the Leningrad funeral of 1935 (Suprematist coffin, a truck with a black square on the radiator along Nevsky Prospect, a rail car to Moscow, cremation at the Donskoy crematorium) and of the burial of the urn at Nemchinovka on 21 May 1935 under an oak, with a wooden cube by Suetin bearing a black square. Also the later history as the article tells it: name banned from 1937, oak felled in 1941, in 1944 only the stump and the brick base found, field ploughed in the 1950s, location claimed to be confirmed by ground-penetrating radar in 2015.
entries.limitation: A science correspondent’s article in a newspaper; no archive is cited for the funeral details. The cross-shaped coffin, the loss of the markers and the radar confirmation are the article’s own statements (its authors belong to the group that searched for the grave). Read through a web-fetch summary (machine summary), with quotations checked against it, not against the full page.

entries.author: Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza
entries.title: Nikolai Suetin (artist biography)
entries.supports: That Suetin decorated Malevich’s coffin with Suprematist motifs and organised his funeral in 1935.
entries.limitation: A museum biography note; one sentence read.

entries.author: Stedelijk Studies research log
entries.title: To Become an Abstraction: Malevich
entries.supports: That Malevich died on 15 May 1935; that photographs show his body in an architecton-shaped coffin among his works, and a family photograph beside a cubic gravestone with the black square at Nemchinovka (1935); that the pupils Rozhdestvensky and Suetin designed the coffin (green, black and white, a red circle at the feet, a black square at the head, the cross left out so as to avoid religious reference), Malevich not having designed it himself, a belief the log calls a legend with some basis; the cube made by Suetin, and the burial on 21 May.
entries.limitation: A research log by Katerina Sidorova (Stedelijk Museum). It gives no citation for the funeral paragraph; its reference list includes Buksha (2013) and it refers to the Khardzhiev archive in general terms. Read through a web-fetch summary (machine summary), not the page in full.

entries.author: Razova, I. I.
entries.title: Похоронный обряд Белозерского района Вологодской области
entries.title_en: The funeral rite of Belozersk district, Vologda oblast
entries.publisher: booksite.ru/folk (reprint; journal and year not given in the text read)
entries.supports: Local practice from named informants born 1898–1935 in villages of Belozersk district: mirrors covered for forty days; coins placed on the window and thrown into the grave to ‘buy’ the burial place; the door not bolted for forty days because the dead is believed to return until the fortieth day; the body kept three days on a bench.
entries.limitation: No year or journal in the text read; informants’ birth years date the memory to the twentieth century, not the recording. A regional description, not a general rule.

entries.author: Great Russian Encyclopedia (entry author not read)
entries.title: Восточнославянская похоронная обрядность
entries.title_en: East Slavic funeral rite
entries.supports: The entry’s statement that the East Slavic funeral rite is on the whole uniform and stable, with local variation touching only surface levels, and that it includes cleansing and protective acts (mirrors covered, objects overturned, hands washed after the cemetery) and prohibitions.
entries.limitation: Only the search extract was read, not the whole entry; the extract gives no author.

entries.author: Butovo Firing Range memorial (martyr.ru, church-run site)
entries.title: Butovo — booklet (English)
entries.supports: The site’s statement that Butovo is the largest place of mass shootings and burials of victims of Stalinist repression in the Moscow region, that 20,760 names are known, that the shootings fell between August 1937 and October 1938, and that the range operated from 1934 to 1953.
entries.limitation: A memorial site run by the church; the count is the site’s own and other pages read give 20,761, 20,762 and 20,765, which the atlas does not reconcile.

entries.author: Great Russian Encyclopedia (entry author not read)
entries.title: Бутовский полигон
entries.title_en: Butovo firing range
entries.supports: About 20.8 thousand people executed and buried at Butovo from August 1937 to October 1938, of whom 19.9 thousand men, over 80% non-party, and over 2.5 thousand prisoners of Dmitlag.
entries.limitation: Only the search extract was read.

entries.author: Meduza editors
entries.title: «Бессмертный полк» попал в окружение
entries.title_en: The Immortal Regiment got surrounded
entries.supports: On 9 May 2012 six thousand Tomsk residents walked with portraits of their relatives; the action reached about 140 places by 2013 and about 450 by 2014; a dispute over who controls the name.
entries.limitation: Journalism with a position on the dispute; only the opening of the article was read.

entries.author: Culture.ru object overview (compiler not named in the extract read)
entries.title: Похоронный обряд в традиции Средней Сухоны
entries.title_en: The funeral rite in the tradition of the Middle Sukhona
entries.supports: Middle Sukhona (eastern Vologda oblast): elders preparing death clothes in advance; water after washing poured out in a special way at the house corner, in the yard and at crossroads; bench or table lined and covered with white cloth torn by hand; soap from the washing used to calm a restless family member or animal; a towel hung at the house corner until the fortieth day.
entries.limitation: Only extracts from search results were read; the page could not be fetched. The compiler and fieldwork dates are not known to the atlas.

entries.author: Adonyeva, S. (interview)
entries.title: «Ух, был да и нету, был да и нету»: антрополог — о русских традициях похорон
entries.title_en: ‘He was and now he’s gone’: an anthropologist on Russian funeral traditions
entries.supports: S. Adonyeva’s description, from the Vologda tradition recorded in the late 20th and early 21st centuries, that the water, washcloth and soap used to wash the dead are destroyed so that they cannot be used in harmful magic.
entries.limitation: A popular interview; one fact was read from a fetched summary, not from the full page.

entries.author: Great Russian Encyclopedia (entry author not read)
entries.title: Восточнославянская похоронная обрядность
entries.title_en: East Slavic funeral rite
entries.supports: That washing is an obligatory element of the funeral-memorial rite, that the dead are dressed in the best or in prepared death clothes, and that specially hired people may wash and dress the body and make the coffin.
entries.limitation: Only the search extract was read.

entries.author: Zelenin, D. K. (preface), in a 2024 Eksmo reissue read online
entries.title: Мертвецы и русалки. Очерки славянской мифологии (предисловие)
entries.title_en: Corpses and Rusalkas: Essays on Slavic Mythology (preface)
entries.publisher: Eksmo, via Yandex Books online reader
entries.supports: Zelenin’s own account of how the study began: fieldwork among the Besermyans of Vyatka province in summer 1909, the offering called kuyas’kon made with contempt and fear to people dead prematurely by unnatural death, a first article of 1911 in Zhivaya starina, and its growth into the book.
entries.limitation: Only the preface extract in the online reader was read. The reissue’s title and editing differ from the 1916 edition (Petrograd, A. V. Orlov), which was not consulted directly.

entries.author: Wikisource contributors
entries.title: Умершие неестественной смертью и русалки (Зеленин) — оглавление
entries.title_en: Zelenin, The Dead by Unnatural Death and Rusalki — contents
entries.supports: Bibliographic data of the first edition: Zelenin, Ocherki russkoi mifologii, vol. 1, Petrograd, A. V. Orlov, 1916, 328 pp.
entries.limitation: The contents table was not legible in the extract; only the imprint was read.

entries.author: Danilov, P. G.
entries.title: Погребальная практика русского населения Тобольского Прииртышья в XVIII—XIX веках: случаи отступления от официального законодательства
entries.title_en: Burial practice of the Russian population of the Tobolsk Irtysh region in the 18th–19th centuries: cases of deviation from official legislation
entries.supports: Legal frame (Senate decree of 24 Dec 1771, extended by the Tobolsk consistory to villages; Synod decree of 12 Apr 1833 on burials in closed cemeteries), two archival cases from the Tobolsk Spiritual Consistory fund (1774, 1815), 19 petitions of 1912–13, and the 2015 excavation of two infant burials at the abandoned village of Yarkova.
entries.limitation: Read through a fetched summary of the open-access PDF, not page by page; the article itself is inconsistent about the family in the 1774 case. The infant plot interpretation (a family cemetery of unbaptized children) is the authors’ own (Danilov and Turova 2017), based on two burials only.

entries.author: Yugai, E. F.
entries.title: Актуализируя причитания: взгляд причитальщицы на импровизацию в конце ХХ–ХХI вв.
entries.title_en: Actualizing the lament: the lamenter’s view of improvisation, late 20th–21st centuries
entries.supports: Interview and narrative material from Vologda Oblast (Kaduy, Totma, Nikolsk, Belozersk and Vozhega districts; informants mostly women born in the 1920s–1940s): two kinds of lamenter, the paid specialist and the bereaved relative; hidden preparation behind an appearance of spontaneity; the lament’s role in moving the dead into the status of ancestor and in regulating grief; and the author’s contrast with Barsov’s 1872 reading.
entries.limitation: Read through a fetched summary of the open-access PDF, not page by page. Vologda material only; the article does not speak for other regions. Its argument about Barsov is the author’s reading.

entries.author: N. P. Rozanov
entries.title: O moskovskikh gorodskikh kladbishchakh
entries.title_en: On Moscow city cemeteries
entries.year: 1868 (offprint from the June issue of Dushepoleznoe chtenie, 1868; censor’s permission dated 8 June 1868)
entries.publisher: Moscow, Universitetskaia tipografiia (Katkov i Ko.), 16 pp.; read from the project owner’s scan (DjVu, 16 pages) by OCR, and earlier through azbyka.ru
entries.supports: A decree of 12 April 1722 on lowering tombstones to ground level; the decree of 10 October 1723 (burial at churches only for ‘notable persons’, the rest outside the town; not carried out after Peter’s death in January 1725); Senate decrees of 24 March and 1 November 1771; the new cemeteries Dorogomilovskoe, Vagankovskoe, Miusskoe and Pyatnitskoe; the church at Vagankovo consecrated 1772.
entries.limitation: FULL TEXT READ in OCR of the owner’s scan (old orthography, OCR errors such as ‘1774’ for 24 March 1771). A short popular-historical booklet for the church press, not an archival edition; its decree dates and lists were taken from consistory files that were not seen here. Read closely: pp. 1–6 on the decrees of 1722–23 and 1771–72; the later pages (lists of cemetery churches, 19th-century building) skimmed.

entries.author: Kirillitsa (Rambler Weekend, unsigned)
entries.title: «Голубцы»: что так называли русские
entries.title_en: ‘Golubtsy’: what the Russians called them
entries.supports: That crosses under small roofs can still be seen in Russian cemeteries; that golubets also named a built-in box beside the stove in a peasant house (the article cites Dal for this).
entries.limitation: Popular article without a named author or references. It is used only for the existence of the form and the two meanings of the word; its claims about pagan origins were not used.

entries.author: Kuznetsova, V. P.; Kovyrshina, Yu.
entries.title: I. A. Fedosova i vyrozerskaia shkola prichital’shchits (I. A. Fedosova and the Vyrozero school of lamenters)
entries.publisher: Collection on the folk traditions of the Russian North, Petrozavodsk, pp. 153–163 (copyright line 2000; collection title not shown in the PDF extract read)
entries.supports: What a ‘school’ of lamenters means; learning of lament in childhood; the 40–50-line versus 1,074-line wedding laments; Fedosova’s birthplace district, later residence, and the dates of her melody recordings.
entries.limitation: Full PDF read through a text extract; reading status RELEVANT EXTRACT READ. Concerns Vyrozero and the Zaonezhye only; wedding rather than funeral laments in the length comparison.

entries.author: Grinkova, N. P.
entries.title: Obriad «vozhdenie rusalki» v sele B. Vereika Voronezhskoi oblasti (The rite ‘leading the rusalka’ in the village of Bolshaya Vereika, Voronezh oblast)
entries.publisher: Sovetskaia etnografiia (Etnograficheskoe obozrenie archive), 1947 no. 1, pp. 178–184
entries.supports: A first-hand record of a spring rite in one village (collected 1925 and 1936 from A. K. Baryshnikova): the figure, the procession, the date, the informant’s two reasons, its last performance in 1935.
entries.limitation: Read from a PDF supplied by the project owner (eoarchive_1947_1_178_Grinkova.pdf), text layer with OCR noise, pp. 178–181 read in full; pages 182–184 only skimmed. Grinkova’s comparative frame (dying-and-resurrecting deity, after Frazer) is the author’s theory and is not adopted. The song text is not reproduced. Journal title for 1947 to be confirmed against the archive’s own catalogue.

entries.author: Zelenin, Dmitry K.
entries.title: Vostochnoslavianskaia etnografiia (Russian translation of Russische (Ostslavische) Volkskunde, Berlin–Leipzig 1927), transl. K. D. Tsivina
entries.publisher: Nauka, Glavnaia redaktsiia vostochnoi literatury, Moscow (Etnograficheskaia biblioteka), 511 pp.
entries.supports: A synthesis of Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian funeral practice (washing, death clothes, coffin, carrying out): §132, pp. 345–349 of the 1991 translation, with the groups named where Zelenin names them and citations to the archive of the Russian Geographical Society and to named collectors.
entries.limitation: Read from a PDF supplied by the project owner (text.pdf in the owner’s ‘res’ folder, copy ‘text (1).pdf’), OCR with some errors. Read so far: § 132 (pp. 345–349), § 134 (pp. 352–355), §§ 156–158 (pp. 410–416); the rest of the book is unread. A second-hand synthesis: the archive files behind the details were not seen. Mixes East Slavic groups; the atlas attributes each detail to the group Zelenin names; § 159 (water spirit), p. 416, also read.

entries.author: Dronova, T. I.
entries.title: Tema smerti v kartine mira staroverov-bespopovtsev Ust’-Tsil’my (The theme of death in the world picture of the priestless Old Believers of Ust-Tsilma)
entries.supports: The Ust-Tsilma community’s own lists of ‘clean’ and ‘unclean’ dead, its words for unnatural death, handling and burial of suicides (to the 1970s), and the treatment of unbaptised infants.
entries.limitation: Full text read from a PDF supplied by the project owner (09_dronova.pdf), text layer with minor OCR errors; pp. 201–204 read closely, the rest skimmed. One district of Russian Old Believers without priests; informants are not named (the author uses field materials and family manuscripts whose owners asked for anonymity).

entries.author: Iugai, Elena
entries.title: “From This Place You Cannot Hear Speech. From This Place You Cannot Receive a Letter”: The Letter-Message in Russian Funeral Lamentations
entries.year: after 2016 (year not shown in the PDF)
entries.publisher: Journal not shown in the PDF supplied; pp. 165–184; the Moscow School of Social and Economic Sciences
entries.supports: Eastern Vologda funeral and commemoration laments by occasion; the statement that Barsov’s Olonets performers are not representative; other published Russian lament collections.
entries.limitation: Read from a PDF supplied by the project owner (RY_11_Iugai.pdf); first 6 pages closely, the analysis of the ‘letter-message’ formula and the reference list only skimmed. Journal name and year are not on the pages read and the latest work cited is 2016, so the entry is incomplete until checked against the journal. The description is of eastern Vologda; it makes no claim for all Russia. The lament texts it quotes are not reproduced.

entries.author: Tolstaya, Svetlana M.
entries.title: The Living and the Dead in Slavic Folk Culture: Modes of Interaction between Two Worlds
entries.supports: Regulation of contact between the living and the dead by time, place and means; feeding and inviting the dead; dreams; messages; her argument that the pattern does not fit a simple ‘ancestor cult’.
entries.limitation: Read in full (abstract and sections 1–8) from a PDF supplied by the project owner (religions-15-00566-v2.pdf). Pan-Slavic sample, with Polesie dominant in the protective measures; Russian-specific claims are limited to those she attributes to the Russian North or the East Slavs. Page numbers are as the journal prints them, read from the running heads. Link taken from the PDF’s own citation line (Religions 2024, 15, 566; received 18 February 2024, published 30 April 2024). The passage on house-spirits (pp. 11–12 of 16) re-read on 2026-11-16: she reports that works on Slavic demonology show house-spirits coming from revered ancestors of the family, and describes the Polesie domovik.

entries.author: Sedakova, Irina
entries.title: Unlived Life: The Death and Funeral of a Child in Slavic Traditional Culture
entries.publisher: Folklore: Electronic Journal of Folklore 80, pp. 47–68 (open access)
entries.supports: Slavic beliefs about early and child death; baptism and burial of unbaptised children; coffin customs; the three Russian items cited second-hand.
entries.limitation: Read in full from a PDF supplied by the project owner, for the Russian-attributed passages only; main material is Bulgarian. Russian items are citations to compilations (Listova, Vlasova, Naumenko) that were not seen.

entries.author: Nikolaev, Oleg R.
entries.title: Traditsionnye formuly krest'ianskoi kul'tury na slome epokh: «Pokhoronili khorosho» (k voprosu o fotografiiakh pokhoron)
entries.publisher: pp. 358–370; journal or collection title not shown on the pages read (CyberLeninka copy supplied by the project owner)
entries.supports: The formula ‘buried well’; funeral photographs in family albums, 1950s–1970s; the author’s hypothesis linking them to the war and repression.
entries.limitation: Read in full from the owner’s PDF. Single-author hypothesis from his own fieldwork, not quantified. The journal and issue are to be added. The family ‘spravka’ text he prints (pp. 365–367) is not reproduced here.

entries.author: Dynin, V. I.
entries.title: Nekotorye osobennosti mifologicheskogo obraza rusalki u vostochnykh slavian
entries.publisher: Etnograficheskoe obozrenie 1994, no. 6, pp. 111–121 (open-access scan at eo.iea.ras.ru)
entries.supports: Regional description of the rusalka among East Slavs; the late arrival of the word in the Russian North; the author’s late-origin thesis.
entries.limitation: Read from the owner’s PDF (OCR text) pp. 111–118; pp. 119–121 only skimmed. Page numbers read from running heads and may be off by one. The thesis is the author’s and is contested by the scholars he lists on p. 111. Footnoted sources not seen.

entries.author: Maksimov, S. V.
entries.title: Nechistaia, nevedomaia i krestnaia sila
entries.publisher: St Petersburg: Golike i Vilborg (Ethnographic Bureau of Prince V. N. Tenishev); online copy of the 1994 Polisett reprint, Vologda regional library, supplied by the project owner
entries.supports: A collector’s statements on burial of suicides and on the water spirit and the drowned.
entries.limitation: Read by keyword search in the 13 HTML files (suicide, drowned, rusalka passages only), not the whole book. Page numbers are those marked in the online copy and may not match the 1903 pages. Maksimov died in 1900; the book was finished by editors. Individual items carry no stated place or informant. The bruises-and-scratches passage and the wooden cup with three wax candles fixed to its edges (it sinks and stops over the drowned) were re-read in the owner’s HTML files on 2026-11-16.

entries.author: Moroz, Andrei B.
entries.title: Molitva v broshennom dome: novye apotropeicheskie praktiki?
entries.publisher: Kul'tura slavian i kul'tura evreev: dialog, skhodstva, razlichiia (yearbook; DOI 10.31168/2658-3356.2019.15; begins on p. 247; volume and issue not established)
entries.supports: Three field cases (Arkhangelsk 2015, Bryansk 2016, Arkhangelsk 2017) of protective texts left in houses being abandoned; the author’s hypothesis of a new practice linked to migration.
entries.limitation: Full text read in the built-in browser; on 2026-11-16 the HSE repository copy was re-checked (three cases, matitsa, new practice with unknown spread confirmed; DOI and starting page 247 taken from it; volume and issue still not shown, year from the DOI). Three cases plus a few interviews, no counts; the author says himself that the spread of the practice is unknown. The first text was not seen. Prayer texts quoted in the article are not reproduced here.

entries.author: Yankovskaya, Galina A.
entries.title: Negativnye posledstviia sovetskikh gidroenergeticheskikh proektov: formaty i praktiki memorializatsii
entries.publisher: Sibirskie istoricheskie issledovaniia (open-access text on CyberLeninka)
entries.supports: Formats of commemoration of flooded territories since the 2000s; the author’s reasons for the delay.
entries.limitation: Abstract and conclusion read in the built-in browser; the body (case descriptions) not read line by line. Issue number and pages not shown. Interpretive article on memory, with no counts of villages or graves.

entries.title: Bereg placha
